title: The Panel on Uncertainty: How Teams Adapt
instructions: 阅读下面的文章（约900词），完成10道题。题目类型包括单选、填空、匹配和判断正误/未提及。填空答案必须来自原文，且不超过规定字数。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。本材料为模拟教学材料，不是官方雅思试题。建议先通读全文，再做题。
passage:
A
On a rainy Tuesday in March, a small panel met in a community hall in Bristol. The panel was not a court. It was a group of five people who had agreed to compare how different teams adapt when plans go wrong. The chair, Dr. Maya Chen, opened the meeting with a simple question: “When the future is unclear, what do teams actually do?” The panel had three case studies on the table. Each case described a team facing uncertainty. The goal was not to judge the teams but to compare their strategies. The panel wanted to understand practical responses to unexpected problems, not to assign blame. By examining real examples, they hoped to identify common patterns that other teams could learn from.

B
The first case was about a hospital kitchen. The kitchen served 300 meals a day. One morning, the main oven broke. The head cook, Mr. Patel, had no spare oven. He did not wait for a repair team. Instead, he moved the soup to the small stove and asked two staff members to prepare cold sandwiches. The kitchen still served all 300 meals, but the menu changed. Mr. Patel said, “We lost the baked potatoes, but we kept the service.” The panel noted that this strategy was “improvise with what you have.” It worked because the team had clear roles and quick communication. Everyone knew what to do without needing lengthy instructions. This quick thinking allowed the kitchen to maintain its service despite the broken equipment.

C
The second case was about a small software company. The company had ten employees. They were building a new app for a client. Two weeks before the deadline, the client asked for a major change. The team leader, Ms. Okafor, called a meeting. She did not hide the problem. She said, “We cannot finish everything. We must choose.” The team listed all tasks and marked each one as “must have” or “nice to have.” They dropped three “nice to have” features and finished the “must have” ones on time. The client was happy with the smaller app. The panel called this strategy “reduce scope, protect the core.” By focusing on essential features, the team delivered a functional product and maintained client satisfaction. This approach required careful planning and clear communication about priorities.

D
The third case was about a volunteer group that organized a street festival. The group had 40 volunteers. Two days before the festival, the weather forecast changed. Heavy rain was now expected. The group had no indoor space. The leader, Mr. Silva, did not cancel the event. He asked the volunteers to build simple covers from plastic sheets and to move the sound system under a bridge. He also shortened the festival by two hours. The festival happened. Fewer people came, but no one was hurt. The panel called this strategy “adapt the plan, keep the event.” The volunteers worked together to overcome the weather challenge, showing flexibility and teamwork. Their ability to adjust quickly ensured the event proceeded safely.

E
After the three cases, Dr. Chen asked the panel to compare the strategies. One member, Ms. Grant, said, “All three teams changed something. But they did not change everything.” Another member, Mr. Lee, agreed. He said, “The kitchen changed the menu. The software team changed the features. The festival group changed the time and the space. In each case, the team kept the main goal.” The panel wrote a short list of common actions: (1) talk early, (2) list what is essential, (3) use what you have, and (4) protect people first. These actions were seen as key to successful adaptation under pressure.

F
However, the panel also found differences. The kitchen had no time to plan. Mr. Patel acted in minutes. The software team had two weeks, so they could plan carefully. The festival group had two days, so they had some time but not much. Dr. Chen said, “Time changes the strategy. With more time, you can choose. With less time, you must act.” The panel agreed that time was a key factor. The amount of time available influenced how each team approached the problem and the solutions they chose.

G
Finally, the panel discussed what did not work. In a fourth case, which was not on the table, a team had no clear leader. When a problem appeared, everyone waited for someone else. The team lost two days. The panel did not study this case in detail, but they mentioned it as a warning. Dr. Chen said, “Uncertainty is not the main problem. The main problem is not knowing who decides.” This example highlighted the importance of clear leadership in times of crisis.

H
The meeting ended with a short report. The report had three sentences: “Teams adapt best when they talk early. They must know what is essential. They must protect people first.” The panel did not claim that these rules work in every situation. They only said that these rules helped the three teams in the case studies. The report was sent to a local training center. The panel planned to meet again in June to compare more cases. The findings were intended to provide practical guidance for teams facing uncertainty.

grammar.title: 名词单复数、拼写、数字和大小写；问句结构复查
grammar.explanation: 英语中，可数名词有单数和复数形式。单数前常用 a/an 或 the；复数一般加 -s 或 -es，如 team → teams, box → boxes。注意不规则复数，如 person → people, child → children。数字要写清楚：300 读作 three hundred；日期和月份首字母大写，如 June。问句结构：一般疑问句把 be 动词或助动词提前，如 “Did he wait?”；特殊疑问句用 “疑问词 + 助动词 + 主语 + 动词”，如 “What did Mr. Patel do?”。注意主谓一致和大小写。
grammar.example: The kitchen served 300 meals a day.

The team having a clear leader.
The team have clear leader.
answers: The team has a clear leader.
